title: Statute of Frauds (Title 32, Chapter 3)
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page
legal_subject: Contract enforceability: which agreements must be in writing
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov
what_it_says_and_notes: No action may be brought on five listed categories of agreement (including an agreement not to be performed within one year, and promises to answer for another's debt) unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. Site discloses the unannotated Code is not the official version.

title: Limitation of Civil Actions, general contract periods (Title 15, Chapter 3)
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page
legal_subject: Breach of contract: time limit to sue
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov (via the no-www address of the same page)
what_it_says_and_notes: § 15-3-530(1): three years for an action on a contract, obligation or liability, express or implied, excepting those in § 15-3-520. § 15-3-520(b): twenty years for sealed instruments, except a sealed contract for sale of goods follows § 36-2-725. Editor's note: the period was reduced from six to three years in 1988.

title: Contract provision shortening the statutory period (Title 15, Chapter 3)
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page
legal_subject: Contract clauses that shorten the time to sue
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov
what_it_says_and_notes: A contract clause (verbal or written) saying a party is barred from suing unless suit is brought in less time than the statute of limitations does not bar the action if it is brought within the statutory period. PRODUCT USE: a rule your analyzer can flag. Clauses that try to shorten the time to sue should be marked as likely ineffective under SC law, with this section as the source.

title: Commercial Code: Sales (UCC Article 2), Title 36, Chapter 2
date_or_version: Current unannotated Code as shown on page (Copyright notice 2026)
legal_subject: Contracts for the sale of goods: writing requirement, modification, unconscionability, warranty disclaimers, excuse, limiting remedies and damages
verification_status: Verified: page text read directly on scstatehouse.gov (sections 36-2-101 through 36-2-723 read)
what_it_says_and_notes: § 36-2-102: applies to transactions in goods. § 36-2-201: writing required for goods of $500 or more, with exceptions. § 36-2-209: modification needs no consideration; no-oral-modification clauses are enforceable with limits. § 36-2-302: court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable contract or clause. § 36-2-316: warranty disclaimers must mention merchantability and be conspicuous. § 36-2-718: liquidated damages must be reasonable or are void as a penalty. § 36-2-719: remedies may be limited; consequential damages may be limited unless unconscionable. Applies to GOODS, not services.

title: Statute of limitations in contracts for sale
legal_subject: Time limit to sue on a sales-of-goods contract
verification_status: Verified: full section text read on Justia (secondary host). The official scstatehouse.gov chapter page (row 4) contains the same section, which my read of it stopped short of (it ended at § 36-2-724)
what_it_says_and_notes: § 36-2-725(1): six years after the cause of action accrues for breach of any contract for sale. (2): warranty claims accrue when the breach is or should have been discovered. Resolves the conflict in secondary sources (some said four years): the answer is six years, confirmed by the Supreme Court in row 6. Compare the three-year general rule in row 2.

title: Ashley II of Charleston, L.L.C. v. PCS Nitrogen, Inc.
citation: Opinion No. 27420 (S.C. July 23, 2014) (reporter citation not yet confirmed)
legal_subject: Indemnity clauses covering the indemnitee's own negligence
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on Justia (secondary host)
what_it_says_and_notes: States that the Court has long recognized the rule that a contract of indemnity is not construed to indemnify the indemnitee against losses from its own negligent acts unless that intention is expressed in clear and unequivocal terms (quoting Laurens Emergency Med. Specialists, PA v. M.S. Bailey & Sons Bankers, 355 S.C. 104, 111, 584 S.E.2d 375, 379 (2003); the opinion prints the name as 'Baily'). The holding itself is narrow: the rule did not bar indemnity for strict-liability CERCLA costs. The rule is background, so the primary source to add next is Laurens. Policy reason given: deterring negligence. Also stresses freedom of sophisticated businesses to allocate risk by contract. Subsequent-history check not completed.

title: Herron v. Century BMW
citation: No. 26805 (S.C. Apr. 19, 2010) (reporter citation not yet confirmed)
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on FindLaw (secondary host)
what_it_says_and_notes: Restates the South Carolina unconscionability test from Simpson v. MSA of Myrtle Beach, Inc., 373 S.C. 14, 25, 644 S.E.2d 663, 668 (2007): absence of meaningful choice due to one-sided provisions, together with terms so oppressive that no reasonable person would make them and no fair and honest person would accept them. Meaningful-choice factors include bargaining-power disparity, relative sophistication, whether the party is a substantial business concern, surprise, and conspicuousness. Notes a strong presumption favoring arbitration agreements and that adhesion contracts are not per se unconscionable. CONSUMER context (car purchase): this does not decide a business-to-business dispute. Simpson itself was read only as quoted here. Subsequent-history check not completed.

title: Copyright Act: Ownership of copyright
issuing_authority: United States Congress (U.S. Code, 2024 Edition, via GPO)
legal_subject: Who owns copyright in designs and artwork
verification_status: Verified: section text read on govinfo.gov
what_it_says_and_notes: § 201(a): copyright vests initially in the author. § 201(b): for a work made for hire, the employer or person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author and owns the rights unless the parties agree otherwise in a signed writing. § 201(d): ownership may be transferred by any means of conveyance. NOT YET REVIEWED: the definition of work made for hire in 17 U.S.C. § 101 (decides whether commissioned designs qualify) and § 204(a) (writing requirement for transfers). Add both before relying on this for an ownership analysis.

title: Gladden v. Boykin
legal_subject: Limitation of liability: caps enforceable? Public policy and unconscionability
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion, majority and dissent, read on Hall Approved (secondary host built from CourtListener data)
what_it_says_and_notes: 3-2 decision. Majority enforced a clause limiting a home inspector's liability to the fee paid, holding it did not violate public policy as expressed by the General Assembly and was not unconscionable; said limitation clauses are routinely entered into and commercially reasonable in at least some cases. Two Justices dissented, arguing a nominal cap is unconscionable and against public policy in a consumer professional-services contract. A list of 10 later cases cites it; their treatment of it was not reviewed.

title: Maybank v. BB&T Corp.
legal_subject: Limitation of liability clauses: general enforcement, strict construction, limits
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on Hall Approved (secondary host)
what_it_says_and_notes: Held a clause barring consequential, indirect, special and punitive damages enforceable against a sophisticated trust advisor. States the Court has generally upheld limitation of liability and exculpatory clauses as commercially reasonable (citing Gladden), but the law disfavors them and courts strictly construe them against the drafter; a clause may be declared unenforceable if it violates public policy or is unconscionable; courts rely on legislative enactments to find public policy; bargaining disparity alone was not enough. The clause did not strip all damages. Also held that a finding of constructive fraud (as opposed to actual fraud) did not defeat the clause. Subsequent-history check not completed.

title: Maximum rate of interest; legal rate of interest (Consumer Protection Code)
legal_subject: Interest rates in written contracts; late-payment interest
verification_status: Verified: full section text read on Justia (secondary host). The official scstatehouse.gov page was not read
what_it_says_and_notes: (1) No more than six percent per annum may be charged on a contract for the hiring, lending, or use of money or other commodity, EXCEPT upon written contracts in which, by express agreement, any rate of interest may be charged, except as otherwise provided in this title or by law. (2) 'Legal rate of interest' in a document means the rate in § 34-31-20 unless the document says otherwise. Other limits 'in this title or by law' (for example consumer-credit rules or unconscionability) were not researched. The § 34-31-20(A) legal rate of 8.75% per annum applies when no written agreement fixes another rate; that figure is quoted in Maybank (row 13).

title: Burnett Dubose Co. v. Starnes
issuing_authority: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
legal_subject: Contractual late-payment charges versus the statutory legal rate
authority_type: Case (S.C. Court of Appeals precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on Hall Approved (secondary host)
what_it_says_and_notes: Held that the statutory rate on accounts stated (§ 34-31-20) applies only in the absence of a written agreement fixing a different rate, and enforced a signed invoice term of 1.5% per month (18% per year) on past-due accounts. title: Sermons v. Caine & Estes Insurance Agency, Inc.
legal_subject: Covenants not to compete: enforceability test
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on Justia (secondary host)
what_it_says_and_notes: Restrictive covenants are disfavored and strictly construed against the employer. Enforceable only if necessary to protect a legitimate interest, reasonably limited in time and place, not unduly harsh and oppressive in curtailing the person's ability to earn a livelihood, reasonable from the standpoint of sound public policy, and supported by valuable consideration. The Court held three covenants (employment and shareholder-sale) unenforceable: a limit 'at any time' could not be justified, a statewide restriction had no good reason, though two or three years may not be obnoxious. LIMIT: an employee/shareholder case. The sample clause instead stops a customer from buying printing elsewhere in the state for five years after the term, and whether courts apply this test to such a restraint was not researched. Subsequent-history check not completed.

title: Carolina Cable Network v. Alert Cable TV, Inc.
citation: 447 S.E.2d 199 (S.C. 1994) (reporter citation to S.C. Reports not yet confirmed)
legal_subject: Termination rights: notice and good faith
authority_type: Case (binding precedent, if still good law)
verification_status: Verified: full opinion read on Justia (secondary host)
what_it_says_and_notes: A contract with no definite duration is terminable by either party on reasonable notice (quoting Childs v. City of Columbia, 87 S.C. 566, 70 S.E. 296 (1911)). Terminations are judged for reasonableness and found wrongful only in extraordinary circumstances: arbitrary, malicious, or bad faith conduct. A termination motivated by a legitimate business reason (a price far below market) was reasonable. Cites Philadelphia Storage Battery Co. v. Mutual Tire Stores, 161 S.C. 487, 159 S.E. 825 (1931) (distributor terminated at the height of the selling season without notice), not yet read. LIMIT: the sample contract has a fixed three-year term with a seven-day, no-cause exit for Provider only, which this case does not decide. Subsequent-history check not completed.

title: Act No. 159 of 2024 (S. 434): automatic renewal provisions in service contracts
legal_subject: Automatic renewal clauses: consumer notice rules
verification_status: Verified: enacted bill text read on scstatehouse.gov. The codified sections themselves were not read
what_it_says_and_notes: An automatic renewal provision in a service contract is not enforceable against the contract holder unless the holder was given written or electronic notice 30 to 60 days before the cancellation deadline that conspicuously discloses the renewal, the amount charged on renewal, and how to cancel. 'Automatic renewal provision' means a renewal of more than one month that keeps the contract in effect more than six months after it began. IMPORTANT LIMIT: for the Title 37 version, 'service contract' excludes contracts offered to anyone other than an individual for personal, family or household purposes, so it appears NOT to cover a business customer such as the sample's bakery LLC. The Title 38 version (§ 38-78-55) depends on that chapter's own definition of 'service contract,' which was not read.
